The operating system and Kubernetes upgrade on separate axes. To move the OS,
you boot a new image. This has one mechanism and one rollback path. To move
Kubernetes, you use `kubernetes.version` or `cctl k8s upgrade`, and you need no
new image. [Upgrading Kubernetes specifically](#upgrading-kubernetes-specifically)
below covers it. Only one operation is not symmetric: to roll a Kubernetes
version *back*. k0s does not support a downgrade of a minor.

This page tells you how to:

- Move one node to a new image.
- Roll a whole cluster, one node at a time.
- Roll back when an image is wrong.
- Choose the tag that a node follows.
- Verify the image that you are about to boot.

It applies to every Corium node, for every install path: ISO, qcow2, cloud
image, or an image that you derived yourself.

---

## The model

A Corium node runs an image. An upgrade replaces that image and reboots. There
is no in-place package upgrade, no `k0s` binary to swap, and no second
mechanism that can move the Kubernetes version independently of the OS.

For this last reason, [Corium does not use k0s Autopilot](/docs/reference/feature-support/#out-of-scope).
Autopilot upgrades Kubernetes by replacing the k0s binary on disk. The Corium
binary is in the read-only `/usr`. Two mechanisms that can each change the
version on their own are worse than one that cannot.

### What survives

| Path | Across an upgrade |
|---|---|
| `/usr` | Replaced in full. It is the image |
| `/etc` | Three-way merge. Your edits stay, and the image defaults update around them |
| `/var` | Untouched. `/var/lib/k0s`, container storage, the cluster CA, your data |

This was tested on a live node. After the image switch and the reboot, the
cluster CA was still in place, and the node kept its name.
`corium-bootstrap.service` did not run. The marker in `/var/lib/corium` stayed,
so the node did not try to bootstrap itself a second time.

All results below come from measurements on a three-controller cluster, not
from assumptions.

---

## Upgrading a node

### Before you start

- A node on which you can run `sudo`, locally or over SSH.
- An image tag. See [choosing what to track](#choosing-what-to-track).
- For the `cctl` path only: the [management API](/docs/reference/cli/) enabled on that node,
  and a client certificate for it.

```bash
# See what is running and what, if anything, is staged.
sudo bootc status

# Pull a newer build of the image this node already tracks.
sudo bootc upgrade

# Or move it to a different image or tag.
sudo bootc switch ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:0.5
```

From your workstation, `cctl upgrade <node> --image ...` does the same thing.
It also drains and reboots the node. See [cctl](/docs/reference/cli/).

By default, neither command reboots. They stage a deployment for the next boot.
Thus you choose the maintenance window:

```
Queued for next boot: ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:0.5
  Version: 0.5.0
  Digest: sha256:38c2194904b1de400a6f2366760c85dae5e45bb7f5f500612bb428817e850bb6
```

To reboot immediately, add `--apply`. Or reboot when you are ready.

### Only the difference is transferred

This output comes from a real switch between two builds of this image:

```
layers already present: 65; layers needed: 11 (214.0 MB)
Deploying...done (15 seconds)
```

The switch moved 214 MB for an image of approximately 2.3 GB. The layers that
the two builds share were already on disk. This is the practical argument for an
OS that is an OCI image. Upgrades are incremental for the same reason that
application images are, and there is no custom delta format to maintain.

## Upgrading a cluster

Nodes are replaceable, but the control plane still has a quorum that you must
keep.

### One node at a time

If the [management API](/docs/reference/cli/) is enabled, one command does the whole
sequence for a list of nodes:

> **Warning.** `cctl upgrade` refuses an image that the signing policy of the
> node accepts without a signature. This stops a typo from rebasing a Kubernetes
> node onto a desktop image. It is also the first problem that you meet when you
> derive your own image. Your repository falls under the permissive default of
> the policy. Thus `cctl upgrade` refuses it until you sign it and declare it in
> the policy. See [building your own image](/docs/guides/derived-images/). If you run
> `bootc switch` by hand, it does not do this check.

```bash
cctl upgrade node-1 node-2 node-3 --image ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:<tag>
```

Before it changes any node, the command makes sure that each node meets these
conditions:

- The node is reachable.
- The node is safe to lose: it is bootstrapped, k0s runs, and greenboot did not
  mark the last boot as bad.
- The node is in the same cluster as the others.
- The node is listed only once.
- The node accepts the image under its own signing policy.

If one node fails a check, the command stops and changes nothing. Thus you find
a wrong address or a refused image before the first nodes reboot. To run only
that check, add `--dry-run`.

Then the command takes the nodes in order, and asks each node again if it is
safe to lose. It **stops at the first node that does not come back on the digest
it was sent to**, and tells you how many nodes it upgraded.

Both of these behaviors are deliberate. A rollout that continues past a broken
machine turns one outage into an outage of the whole cluster. Also, a
half-upgraded cluster needs a decision from a person. It is not a number to
hide.

Without the API, do the same sequence by hand:

```bash
# 1. Stop scheduling and move the workloads off.
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# 2. Stage the new image and reboot into it.
ssh <node> sudo bootc switch ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:<tag>
ssh <node> sudo systemctl reboot

# 3. Wait for it to come back Ready, then let it take work again.
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready node/<node> --timeout=5m
kubectl uncordon <node>
```

After the drain and the reboot, the node comes back in approximately 45 seconds
and rejoins on its own. It does not bootstrap again, because the marker in
`/var/lib/corium` stops it.

### Controllers

With three controllers, you can lose one and keep etcd quorum. Thus upgrade
them one at a time, and wait for `Ready` between each one. Never stop two of the
three controllers at the same time. If you do, the cluster loses quorum, and the
API server stops accepting writes.

`cctl upgrade` and `cctl k8s upgrade` enforce this rule. Before and after each
controller, they make sure that every etcd member is healthy. If a member is
not healthy, they stop. See
[etcd around controllers](/docs/reference/cli/#etcd-around-controllers).

With five controllers, the cluster survives two at a time. With two controllers,
the cluster has no quorum to spare, and it is unavailable during each reboot.

If you use [HA](/docs/reference/configuration/#39-ha), a reboot of the controller that holds the
virtual IP moves the virtual IP to another controller. Clients that point at the
VIP reconnect on their own. This failover was tested with a hard stop of the
controller that held the VIP.

## A node that breaks rolls itself back

Nodes run [greenboot](https://github.com/fedora-iot/greenboot) health checks at
boot. If a check fails and there is a previous deployment to return to, the
node rolls back on its own. Thus you can stage an image and reboot without
supervision.

This table comes from a test with an image whose health check always fails:

| Boot | Check | What greenboot does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | fails | First failure. Sets the boot counter to 3 |
| 2 | fails | Counter at 2, reboots to try again |
| 3 | fails | Counter at 1, reboots to try again |
| 4 | fails | Counter at zero. Starts the rollback, which succeeds |
| 5 | healthy | `greenboot health-check passed`, `boot_success=1` |

`GREENBOOT_MAX_BOOT_ATTEMPTS` in `/etc/greenboot/greenboot.conf` sets the
count. After the rollback, the next upgrade replaces the image that failed. Thus
the node does not switch back and forth between the two images. A rollback also
occurs only if an upgrade staged something. If a check fails on a node that
nobody upgraded, you get a warning and must act manually. The node does not
move to an older image without warning.

To add your own checks, put executables in `/etc/greenboot/check/required.d/`.
A non-zero exit fails the boot.

Corium ships one check: is k0s running and answering? It does not require the
node to be `Ready` in Kubernetes, on purpose. A node can be NotReady for reasons
that the image cannot fix, for example:

- No CNI is installed yet.
- A control plane is still coming back.
- The whole cluster has a problem.

An OS rollback fixes none of these. It only takes a healthy machine out of
service at the worst possible moment. A health check that is too strict is worse
than no check. The check gives k0s five minutes to start, because k0s needs time
to unpack its supervised binaries and start etcd. On a node that was never
bootstrapped, the check always passes.

## Rolling back

```bash
sudo bootc rollback
sudo systemctl reboot
```

Or remotely, if the node still answers:

```bash
cctl rollback <node>     # marks the previous image; does not reboot
```

`cctl rollback` stops there on purpose. When you need it, you already have a
problem. A reboot of the node at a moment that you did not choose does not help.
You schedule the reboot.

A rollback is instant and downloads nothing: `Next boot: rollback deployment`.
It changes the order of the boot entries for the deployment that you run and
the previous deployment. Both are already on disk.

A rollback is also symmetric. The image that you left becomes the new rollback
target. If you run the rollback again, you return to where you were. This was
tested in both directions on a live controller.

```bash
sudo bootc status   # shows booted, staged and rollback
```

Two things rollback does **not** undo:

- **Anything written to `/var`.** If a Kubernetes version migrated etcd data,
  an older image does not reverse the migration. Before you skip Kubernetes
  minor versions, read the k0s release notes.
- **Cluster state.** Rolling back one node does not roll back the cluster.

## Choosing what to track

Each release publishes a ladder of tags. Thus each node can choose how much
change it accepts.

| Tag | Moves | You get |
|---|---|---|
| `corium@sha256:...` | Never | Exactly one image. The strongest pin |
| `corium:0.5.0` | Never | One release |
| `corium:0.5` | On patch releases | Fixes, no new behavior |
| `corium:latest` | On every release | Whatever is newest |
| `corium:main` | On every push to `main` | Development builds, unreleased |

**Track `0.5`.** It moves only on patch releases, which do not change
behavior. Thus the node gets fixes without a decision from you. If you prefer to
choose the moment yourself, pin `0.5.0` exactly. Before you move to `0.6`, read
the changelog. A minor release can require a configuration change, and the
changelog names it.

> **Moving from `0.4` to `0.5` changes a node's posture.** From 0.5.0, the
> management API is on by default. A node that names no `api:` block serves its
> enrolment route during the minute between boot and bootstrap. The pairing code
> on its console protects that route. To keep the old behavior, set
> `api.enabled: false`. For this reason, the change is a minor release and not a
> patch. Nothing on the `0.4` rung moves, so a node gets it only when you tell it
> to. See [ADR 11](/docs/decisions/adr-0011-api-on-by-default/).

The ladder does not offer three things:

- There is no major rung below 1.0. Semantic versioning lets a `0.y` minor
  release break things. A `0` tag promises a stability that the version number
  does not give.
- `latest` tells you which release is newest. It does not tell you about
  compatibility. It crosses the minor releases, which is where breaking changes
  occur. Do not run a cluster on it.
- Prereleases publish only their exact tag. `0.5.0-rc.1` never becomes `0.5` or
  `latest`. Thus a node that follows a stable tag does not get a release
  candidate.

`bootc status` always reports the digest that the node booted, whatever the tag
pointed to at that time. During an incident, this is the information that you
need.

### Unattended upgrades

By default, a node does nothing on its own. A Kubernetes node that reboots
without a request causes an outage that nobody scheduled. Thus the image masks
`bootc-fetch-apply-updates.timer`.

If you want more, two levels are available:

```yaml
corium:
  upgrades:
    automatic: download      # none (default) | download | apply
    schedule: "Mon *-*-* 03:00:00"   # systemd OnCalendar, default daily
```

| Policy | What the node does | Reboots itself |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | Nothing. The default | No |
| `download` | Stages a newer image and queues it for the next boot, whenever that is | **No** |
| `apply` | Stages it and reboots | **Yes** |

**`download` is the one most clusters want.** The fetch and the deployment
occur without supervision. Thus the reboot that you schedule is almost instant,
because the slow part is already done. You still choose the moment, drain
first, and do one node at a time.

`apply` drains the node before it reboots. It cordons the node, evicts the pods,
reboots into the staged image, and uncordons the node when k0s is back. Thus a
node that upgrades itself moves its workloads to other nodes and does not kill
them.

These behaviors are deliberate:

- **A drain that cannot finish cancels the upgrade.** When a pod disruption
  budget refuses an eviction, the system works correctly. It is not a fault. The
  node uncordons itself and stays on its current image. The new image stays
  staged, and the node tries again at the next scheduled run. A reboot that
  ignores a PDB defeats the purpose of the PDB.
- **A plain worker reboots without a drain.** A drain needs cluster admin
  credentials, and only a node that runs a control plane has them locally. On
  `worker` nodes, `apply` reboots without a drain. On those nodes, use
  `download`, and start the reboot from a machine that can talk to the API.
- **A single-node cluster also reboots without a drain.** A drain of the only
  node has nowhere to move its pods. Eviction then blocks on their disruption
  budgets, and the drain never finishes. Under the rule above, this cancels
  every upgrade. Thus a `single` node (or any cluster of one) skips the drain
  and reboots directly into the staged image. Its pods come back when the node
  does. This lets `cctl upgrade` reboot a one-node cluster. Otherwise, the image
  stays staged forever.
- **The new image stays locked until the drain succeeds.** `apply` stages with
  `bootc upgrade --download-only`, which leaves the deployment *locked for
  finalization*. It unlocks the deployment with `--from-downloaded` only after
  the node is drained. A reboot for a different reason in between can come from
  an operator, a crash, or a power cut during the drain. After such a reboot,
  the node comes back on the image that it already ran. It does not half-apply
  an upgrade that nobody scheduled.

`schedule` takes any systemd
[OnCalendar](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.time.html)
expression. Corium adds a random delay of up to one hour, so that all nodes do
not contact the registry at the same time. If a node was off, it runs the
missed checks when it starts again. It does not wait for the next window.

To see what a node staged, run:

```bash
sudo bootc status
systemctl list-timers 'corium-upgrade-*' 'bootc-*'
```

## Verifying what you are about to boot

Corium signs every image that it publishes, from a release tag and from `main`.
It uses [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/) in keyless mode. There is no
private key, and the signing identity is the GitHub Actions workflow itself.
The signature is attached to the image digest and not to a tag. Tags move, and
a signature on a moving tag tells you nothing about the image that the tag
points to now.

```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:0.5 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/Corium-OS/Corium/.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```

A successful verification prints this output:

```
Verification for ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:0.5 --
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - Existence of the claims in the transparency log was verified offline
  - The code-signing certificate was verified using trusted certificate
    authority certificates
```

If `cosign verify` stops with no output at all, your registry credential
helper is probably waiting for something. A locked macOS keychain causes this.
To find out, run the command with an empty `DOCKER_CONFIG`:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/emptycfg && echo '{}' > /tmp/emptycfg/config.json
DOCKER_CONFIG=/tmp/emptycfg cosign verify ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:0.5 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/Corium-OS/Corium/.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```

### Nodes enforce it

Corium signs images **twice**, because the two signatures answer different
questions.

| Signature | Proves | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| Keyless | Which workflow run built this image, recorded in a public transparency log | A human, running `cosign verify` |
| Key | That the image came from this project | The node, at pull time |

A Corium node ships a policy that requires the key signature for
`ghcr.io/corium-os/corium`. The public key is at
`/usr/share/corium/cosign.pub`. The node refuses an image from that repository
that is not signed:

```
Source image rejected: A signature was required, but no signature exists
```

The policy is narrow on purpose. Everything else stays permissive, because
k0s pulls its own images from quay.io and docker.io. A policy for all
registries breaks the cluster and does not make it more secure.

To verify the image yourself with the key from a node, run:

```bash
cosign verify --key /usr/share/corium/cosign.pub ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:0.5
```

**Why two signatures rather than one.** A node cannot enforce the keyless
signature. `containers-policy.json` matches a signer by `subjectEmail`, but a
GitHub Actions certificate carries a URI instead. Thus enforcement fails with
`Required email ... not found (got [])`. This is a limitation of
`containers-image`, not a configuration mistake. Know this before you spend
an afternoon on it.

See [bootc: image signatures](https://bootc.dev/bootc/security.html).

## Upgrading Kubernetes specifically

**Most of the time you do not need this section.** With
[ADR 10](/docs/decisions/adr-0010-kubernetes-version-axis/), the Kubernetes version is a
separate axis. Set `kubernetes.version`, or roll a cluster with
`cctl k8s upgrade`. No OS image changes. See
[reference §3.20](/docs/reference/configuration/#320-kubernetes).

This section covers the other axis: how to change the version that an image
*ships*, and the versions for which it accepts extensions. Both are in
`build/k0s.lock`:

```
K0S_FLOOR=v1.36.5+k0s.0

# version         arch    sha256
v1.34.12+k0s.0    amd64   8536acf9...
v1.35.9+k0s.0     amd64   517b88e1...
v1.36.5+k0s.0     amd64   377cdb37...
```

`K0S_FLOOR` is baked into `/usr/bin/k0s`. A node runs this version when its
configuration names no version. The table is the window: the versions for which
this image builds and accepts system extensions. The window is three minors
wide. To change the floor, rebuild the image and roll it out as described above.
To add a version to the window, merge the change. Then the extension is
published, and any node can ask for it without a new image.

`mise run k0s-window vX.Y.Z+k0s.N` adds a version. It downloads the binaries for
both architectures and hashes them. It does not trust a checksum published next
to the download. Review the resulting diff, because every later build verifies
against it.

CI makes sure that the image ships the floor that the lock file names. Thus a
lock file and an image cannot disagree without a failure.

Before you skip a Kubernetes minor version, read the
[k0s release notes](https://docs.k0sproject.io/stable/releases/). k0s follows
upstream Kubernetes, which does not support skipping minors on the control
plane. A node refuses such a change immediately and does not attempt it.
